name: Old English
catalog_quote: § 10. The rule for the accentuation of uncompounded words is the same in Old English as in the oldest period of the other Germanic languages, viz. the chief stress fell upon the stem-syllable and always remained there even when suffixes and inflexional endings followed it, as beran, to bear; dagas, days, greting, greeting; ...

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Deciding quotation confirmed verbatim in the held Wright & Wright 1914 djvu text at pp. 15-16 §10, with §§11-14 as cited; held Sweet 1905 corroborates. (2) Deciding source is a genuine (if dated, 1914) historical-comparative reference grammar with an Accentuation section, not a pedagogical primer; the better-ranked Glottolog grammars (Campbell 1959, Hogg 1992/2011) are not held and not open, but OE root-initial primary stress with unstressed ge-/be-/for- and verbal prefixes is stated identically in every source opened. (3) fetched sources the open-access Fulk 2014 Introductory Grammar (ACMRS; IU ScholarWorks) to; §22 pp. 14-15 confirms the coding (fixed initial/root stress, strict, prefix exceptions morphological).

sources.quote: '22. Most words are accented on the first syllable. There are two exceptions: (1) the prefix ge- is never stressed, and the prefixes be- and for- almost never; (2) prefixes of verbs are unstressed, so that the primary stress falls on the root syllable, as in aþencan, underwreðian, ætspornan (cf. ǽtspornung). When a verb is stressed on the prefix (and this is rare), as in andswarian, it is because the verb is derived from a noun... Even names taken from Latin sources are almost always stressed on the first syllable.' §23: 'A half-stress falls on some middle and final syllables...'
